draft.title: Intertextuality
card: No text is made from nothing. Writers draw on stories, characters, forms and ideas that came before them.
Intertextuality is the relationship between texts that comes from this sharing. The link may be a retold story, a familiar character, a borrowed form or a repeated idea.
The link works in both directions. Knowing the earlier text can change how we read the later one, and the later text can change how we see the earlier one.
For example, a short story about a lonely lighthouse keeper who waits for a ship that never arrives echoes older tales of patient waiting. A reader who knows those tales may hear extra meaning in it.
draft.remember: Intertextuality is the web of links between texts, and each link can shape how both texts are read.

opts: The relationship between texts that share stories or ideas
The use of one writer's exact words in a new text
The way a text is split into chapters or sections
The effect of a writer's life on the text they write
a.why: Intertextuality is about links between texts, such as shared stories, characters, forms or ideas. It is not limited to copying exact words, because a link can be a retold story or a borrowed form.
a.clue: Think about a relationship between two texts, not one text alone.

b.q: Priya writes a poem about a girl who follows a white rabbit into a hidden world. Readers who know older tales of rabbits that lead people into strange places see extra meaning in her poem. What does this show?
opts: Her poem is linked to earlier texts, which adds meaning
Her poem makes no sense unless readers know older tales
Her poem is weaker because it uses a familiar idea
Her poem turns the older tales into brand new texts
b.why: The poem shares an idea with earlier texts, and knowing them adds meaning for readers. It does not need the older tales to make sense, so saying it makes no sense without them goes too far.
b.clue: Does the link add meaning, or is it needed for any meaning at all?

a.best: The relationship between texts that share stories or ideas

b.best: Her poem is linked to earlier texts, which adds meaning

problems.detail: The clue 'Think about a relationship between two texts' gives the answer away, because only the correct option uses the word 'relationship' or mentions texts sharing anything.
The clue's phrase 'add meaning' appears only in the correct option, so a student can match the words without understanding the idea.

A girl following a white rabbit into a hidden world points straight to Carroll's Alice in Wonderland, not to general 'older tales of rabbits'. Students may read it as an allusion or an appropriation, which belong to later points in the chapter, rather than general intertextuality.

opts: The links between texts that share stories, forms or ideas
The copying of one writer's exact words into a new text
The way a text is divided into chapters or sections
The influence of a writer's own life on their text
a.why: Intertextuality is the relationship between texts through shared stories, characters, forms or ideas. Copying exact words is too narrow, because a link can be a retold story or a borrowed form with no words repeated.
a.clue: Can a connection between texts exist without any repeated words?

b.q: Priya writes a story in which a young person leaves home, faces a hard test and returns changed. Readers who know many older tales with this pattern notice more in it. What does this show?
opts: Her story is linked to earlier texts, shaping how it is read
Her story makes no sense unless readers know older tales
Her story is weaker because it uses a familiar pattern
Her story has copied one earlier text word for word
b.why: The story shares a pattern with many earlier texts, and knowing them changes how readers take it. Saying it makes no sense without them goes too far, because a reader who knows no older tales can still follow it.
b.clue: Could a reader who knows no older tales still follow the story?
